modules.title: ENGR108 L1-2: Introduction / vector notation

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 1 - Introduction
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 2 - vector notation

read: VMLS Preface and start of Chapter 1 (pp. xi, 3)

questions.q: Why does the course treat linear algebra as a tool for applications rather than as abstract proofs?
questions.a: Vectors and matrices are used to represent data (time series, images, features, states) and to compute with it; the goal is to be able to formulate and solve real problems.

questions.q: What is an n-vector, and what does "dimension" mean?
questions.a: An ordered list of n numbers; n is its dimension (size).

questions.q: Name two kinds of real-world data a vector can hold.
questions.a: E.g. a time series of sensor readings, pixel values of an image, a feature vector for a data point, the state of a robot (positions and velocities).

questions.q: Give a robotics example of a vector with 6 entries.
questions.a: E.g. 6 joint angles of an arm, or a 3D position plus 3D velocity.

questions.q: What does the notation x_i mean, and what is the zero vector?
questions.a: x_i is the i-th entry (element); the zero vector has all entries 0.

modules.exercise: In NumPy create np.array([1.,2.,3.]); print its length, its 2nd entry (watch zero-based indexing), and np.zeros(3).
modules.recap: Applied linear algebra = representing real data as vectors/matrices and computing with them. The course builds from vectors to least squares to control and estimation. A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Indexing, dimension and special vectors (zeros, ones, unit vectors) are the vocabulary for everything later.

modules.title: ENGR108 L3: vector examples

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 3 - vector examples

questions.q: Why can an image or a document be treated as a vector?
questions.a: You can stack pixel intensities (or word counts) into one long list of numbers, so vector tools (distance, angle) apply.

questions.q: What is a unit vector e_i?
questions.a: The vector with a 1 in position i and 0 elsewhere.

questions.q: Reflection: state the main idea of this segment in 2-3 sentences. What would you ask the instructor?
questions.a: Personal check. If you cannot summarise it, rewatch the last 5 minutes of the segment and re-read the textbook section.

modules.exercise: Represent the sentence "robots learn robots" as a word-count vector over the vocabulary [robots, learn, from, data].
modules.recap: Many kinds of data become vectors; choosing the representation is the first modeling step.

modules.title: ENGR108 L4-5: addition & scalar mult. / VMLS inner product

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 4-addition & scalar mult.
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 5 - VMLS inner product

questions.q: How is vector addition defined for two n-vectors?
questions.a: Entry by entry: (a+b)_i = a_i + b_i. Both must have the same size.

questions.q: Define the inner product a^T b.
questions.a: Sum of products of corresponding entries: a_1 b_1 + ... + a_n b_n.

questions.q: What is a linear combination of vectors a_1..a_k?
questions.a: beta_1 a_1 + ... + beta_k a_k with scalar coefficients beta_i.

questions.q: What does an inner product with a vector of all ones compute?
questions.a: The sum of the entries.

questions.q: Geometrically, what does a + b look like in 2D?
questions.a: Place b's tail at a's head (parallelogram rule); the sum goes from the origin to the far corner.

modules.exercise: Compute np.dot(a, b) for a=[1,2,3], b=[4,5,6] by hand, then verify in NumPy.
modules.recap: Addition and scalar multiplication generate linear combinations, the basic building block for almost every later idea. The inner product turns two vectors into one number and underlies sums, averages, weighted scores, norms and angles.

modules.title: ENGR108 L6-8: VMLS complexity … VMLS taylor approx & reg

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 6 - VMLS complexity
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 7 - VMLS linear functions
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 8-VMLS taylor approx & reg

questions.q: Roughly how many flops does an inner product of n-vectors take?
questions.a: About 2n flops (n multiplications and n-1 additions).

questions.q: State the superposition property of a linear function f.
questions.a: f(alpha x + beta y) = alpha f(x) + beta f(y).

questions.q: What is the first-order Taylor approximation of f near z?
questions.a: f(x) ≈ f(z) + grad f(z)^T (x - z), an affine function.

questions.q: Why do we count flops?
questions.a: To estimate how computation time scales with problem size independent of the machine.

questions.q: Show that f(x)=a^T x is linear.
questions.a: It's an inner product, so a^T(alpha x + beta y) = alpha a^T x + beta a^T y.

modules.exercise: Linearize f(x)=x^2 around z=3 and compare with f(3.1).
modules.recap: Vector operations cost O(n); flop counts tell you how algorithms scale. Linear functions are exactly inner products with a fixed vector; affine adds a constant. Taylor approximation lets us replace a nonlinear function with an affine one locally; the same idea underlies linearizing robot dynamics in LQR.

modules.title: ENGR108 L9-11: VMLS norm … VMLS std. deviation

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 9 - VMLS norm
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 10 - VMLS distance
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 11-VMLS std. deviation

questions.q: Define the Euclidean norm of x.
Define the distance between a and b.
questions.a: dist(a,b) = ||a - b||.

questions.q: How is the standard deviation of a vector defined?
questions.a: The RMS value of the de-meaned vector: std(x) = ||x - avg(x) 1|| / sqrt(n).

questions.q: Name two properties every norm satisfies.
questions.a: E.g. homogeneity ||alpha x|| = |alpha| ||x||, triangle inequality, nonnegativity, definiteness.

questions.q: What is the nearest-neighbor idea?
questions.a: Pick the data point with smallest distance to the query point.

modules.exercise: Compute the standard deviation of 10 noisy measurements of a constant in NumPy.
modules.recap: The norm measures a vector's size; the RMS value is norm/sqrt(n). Distance = norm of the difference; many algorithms (k-NN, clustering, feature matching) rest on it. Mean and standard deviation summarize location and spread; the std is the norm of the mean-removed signal.

modules.title: ENGR108 L12: VMLS angle

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 12 - VMLS angle

questions.q: How is the angle between nonzero vectors defined?
questions.a: cos(theta) = a^T b / (||a|| ||b||).

questions.q: What does a^T b = 0 tell you?
questions.a: The vectors are orthogonal (90 degrees).

questions.q: What does Cauchy-Schwarz say?
questions.a: |a^T b| <= ||a|| ||b||, so the cosine is between -1 and 1.

modules.exercise: Compute the angle between [1,0] and [1,1] in degrees.
modules.recap: Angles come from normalized inner products. Orthogonality (zero inner product) is key to least squares and QR.

modules.title: ENGR108 L15-16: VMLS linear ind. / VMLS Gram Schmidt algo.

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Intro to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 15-VMLS linear ind.
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 16-VMLS Gram Schmidt algo.

questions.q: When are vectors a_1..a_k linearly independent?
questions.a: When the only combination equal to zero is the one with all coefficients zero.

questions.q: What does orthonormal mean?
questions.a: Vectors are mutually orthogonal and each has norm 1.

questions.q: What is a basis of R^n?
questions.a: A set of n linearly independent n-vectors; every vector is a unique combination of them.

questions.q: What does Gram-Schmidt do?
questions.a: Turns independent vectors into orthonormal ones spanning the same space by subtracting projections on earlier ones and normalizing.

modules.exercise: Run Gram-Schmidt by hand on [1,1] and [1,0].
modules.recap: Independence means no redundancy; a basis gives unique coordinates for every vector. Gram-Schmidt builds orthonormal bases; it is the engine of the QR factorization.

modules.title: ENGR108 L17: VMLS matrix notation

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 17 - VMLS matrix notation

read: VMLS 6.1 Matrices, 6.2 Zero and identity matrices, 6.3 Transpose, addition, and norm

questions.q: What is an m x n matrix?
questions.a: A rectangular array with m rows and n columns.

questions.q: What does the transpose do?
questions.a: Swaps rows and columns: (A^T)_ij = A_ji.

questions.q: What is the identity matrix?
questions.a: Square matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere; I x = x.

modules.exercise: Create a 2x3 matrix in NumPy and print A.T and A.shape.
modules.recap: Matrices organize data and functions; transpose, addition and identity are the basics.

modules.title: ENGR108 L18-20: VMLS matrix vector mult … VMLS selector matrices

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 18-VMLS matrix vector mult
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 19-VMLS matrix vector  ex.
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 20-VMLS selector matrices

questions.q: How do you compute y = A x?
questions.a: y_i = (row i of A) . x, equivalently y = x_1 * col_1 + ... + x_n * col_n.

questions.q: Which matrix computes the average of a vector's entries?
questions.a: The row (1/n) 1^T.

questions.q: What is a selector matrix?
questions.a: A matrix whose rows are unit vectors; A x picks out entries of x.

questions.q: Why is y = A x a linear function?
questions.a: A(alpha x + beta z) = alpha A x + beta A z.

questions.q: Give a matrix that reverses a 3-vector.
questions.a: The anti-diagonal permutation matrix with ones on the anti-diagonal.

modules.exercise: Write the selector matrix that picks entries 1 and 3 of a 4-vector.
modules.recap: Matrix-vector multiplication = inner products with rows = linear combination of columns. Many familiar operations (sum, mean, difference, reversal) are matrix-vector products. Selectors pick, reorder and subsample entries via matrix multiplication.

modules.title: ENGR108 L21-22: VMLS incidence matrix / VMLS convolution

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 21 - VMLS incidence matrix
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 22 - VMLS convolution

questions.q: How is a directed graph's incidence matrix defined?
questions.a: Rows = nodes, columns = edges; +1 at the edge's head, -1 at its tail, 0 elsewhere.

questions.q: What is convolution of two vectors?
questions.a: (a*b)_k = sum over i+j=k+1 of a_i b_j, polynomial-multiplication-like sliding product.

questions.q: What does A^T x give for a potential vector x on nodes?
questions.a: Differences of potentials across each edge.

questions.q: How is convolution a matrix-vector product?
questions.a: a*b = T(b) a where T(b) is a Toeplitz matrix built from b.

modules.exercise: Convolve [1,2,3] with [1,-1] using np.convolve.
modules.recap: Incidence matrices encode graph structure; transposed, they compute differences along edges. Convolution (filtering, smoothing) is linear and can be written with a Toeplitz matrix. It is the core of CNNs later.

modules.title: ENGR108 L23-24: VMLS vector linear func / VMLS linear func models

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 23-VMLS vector linear func
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 24-VMLS linear func models

questions.q: Which functions R^n -> R^m are linear?
questions.a: Exactly f(x) = A x for some m x n matrix A.

questions.q: What is a "linear model" for a relationship near an operating point?
questions.a: An affine approximation using the Jacobian (derivative matrix).

questions.q: How do you find A from f?
questions.a: Its columns are f(e_1), ..., f(e_n).

questions.q: Give an example from physics/engineering.
questions.a: E.g. price elasticity, small-signal circuit models or linearized robot dynamics.

modules.exercise: Linearize f(x)=[x1*x2, x1+x2] at (1,2) by computing its Jacobian.
modules.recap: Every linear vector function is a matrix multiply; the columns are the images of the unit vectors. The derivative matrix gives the best local linear model of a vector function.

modules.title: ENGR108 L25: VMLS linear equations

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 25 - VMLS linear equations

questions.q: How do you write a set of linear equations compactly?
questions.a: A x = b.

questions.q: How many solutions can A x = b have?
questions.a: None, one, or infinitely many.

questions.q: Reflection: state the main idea of this segment in 2-3 sentences. What would you ask the instructor?
questions.a: Personal check. If you cannot summarise it, rewatch the last 5 minutes of the segment and re-read the textbook section.

modules.exercise: Solve [[1,1],[1,-1]] x = [3,1] with np.linalg.solve.
modules.recap: Systems of equations are matrix equations; solvability depends on A's shape and independence.

modules.title: ENGR108 L26: VMLS linear dynamic sys

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 26-VMLS linear dynamic sys

questions.q: Write the linear dynamical system equation.
questions.a: x_{t+1} = A_t x_t (optionally + B_t u_t + c_t).

questions.q: What does the state x_t represent?
questions.a: A vector summarizing everything needed to predict the future.

questions.q: What happens in x_{t+1}=A x_t if all eigenvalues have magnitude < 1?
questions.a: The state decays to zero (stable system).

modules.exercise: Simulate x_{t+1}=A x_t for A=[[0.9,0.2],[-0.2,0.9]] for 50 steps and plot it. (Month 1 practice task.)
modules.recap: Linear dynamical systems model how a state evolves; this is your first look at robot dynamics and control.

modules.title: Practice: Simulate a linear dynamical system
modules.steps: Simulate x(t+1) = A x(t) in a loop and plot what happens when you change A (try rotation-scaling matrices with eigenvalue magnitudes 0.9, 1.0, 1.1).

questions.q: When is x(t+1)=A x(t) stable?
questions.a: When all eigenvalues of A have magnitude less than 1.

questions.q: What does an eigenvalue of magnitude 1 with rotation do?
questions.a: Pure oscillation around the origin without decay.

questions.q: How does this relate to a robot's state?
questions.a: A linearized robot is a linear system around an operating point.

modules.exercise: Plot trajectories for the three A matrices and label stable/unstable.
modules.recap: Linear systems model state evolution; Month 1 milestone: simulate a linear system in a loop and plot it.

modules.title: ENGR108 L27-28: VMLS matrix mult / VMLS matrix mult ex

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 27-VMLS matrix mult
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 28-VMLS matrix mult ex

read: VMLS 10.1-10.2 Matrix-matrix multiplication, Composition of linear functions

questions.q: How is (AB)_ij computed?
questions.a: Inner product of row i of A with column j of B.

questions.q: What does the product AB represent as a function?
questions.a: First apply B then A: (AB)x = A(Bx).

questions.q: Is matrix multiplication commutative?
questions.a: No, AB != BA in general.

questions.q: Give an example where composition of linear functions appears.
questions.a: E.g. rotating then scaling; chaining coordinate transformations.

modules.exercise: Verify that two successive 45-degree rotation matrices equal a 90-degree rotation.
modules.recap: Matrix multiplication composes linear functions; order matters. Chained linear maps multiply as matrices; this is how coordinate-frame transformations compose in robotics.

modules.title: ENGR108 L29: VMLS mtrx pwrs & QR fac

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 29-VMLS mtrx pwrs & QR fac

questions.q: What is A^k used for in dynamical systems?
questions.a: x_t = A^t x_0 gives the state after t steps.

questions.q: What is a QR factorization?
questions.a: A = QR with Q having orthonormal columns and R upper triangular, from Gram-Schmidt.

questions.q: Reflection: state the main idea of this segment in 2-3 sentences. What would you ask the instructor?
questions.a: Personal check. If you cannot summarise it, rewatch the last 5 minutes of the segment and re-read the textbook section.

modules.exercise: Use np.linalg.qr on a random 4x3 matrix and check Q^T Q = I.
modules.recap: Matrix powers propagate dynamics; QR gives an orthonormal basis plus triangular coefficients and is the numerically sound way to solve least squares.

modules.title: Practice: Rotate a 2D point
modules.steps: Write rotate(point, angle) using the 2x2 rotation matrix, and plot a square rotating in 10-degree steps.

questions.q: Write the 2D rotation matrix.
questions.a: [[cos t, -sin t],[sin t, cos t]].

questions.q: What is R(t)^{-1}?
What happens to lengths and angles under rotation?
questions.a: They are preserved.

modules.exercise: Plot 36 rotated squares and check the last one equals the first.
modules.recap: Rotation is a matrix; this will return in kinematics.

modules.title: ENGR108 L30: VMLS left & right inv.

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 30-VMLS left & right inv.

questions.q: What is a left inverse of A?
questions.a: A matrix X with X A = I.

questions.q: When does a left inverse exist?
questions.a: When A has linearly independent columns (tall or square).

questions.q: Reflection: state the main idea of this segment in 2-3 sentences. What would you ask the instructor?
questions.a: Personal check. If you cannot summarise it, rewatch the last 5 minutes of the segment and re-read the textbook section.

modules.exercise: Find a left inverse of [[1],[1]] and check it.
modules.recap: Left inverses recover x from y = A x when columns are independent; right inverses give solutions when rows are independent.

modules.title: ENGR108 L31-32: VMLS solving linear eqs / VMLS pseudo inverse

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 31-VMLS solving linear eqs
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 32 - VMLS pseudo inverse

questions.q: When is a square matrix invertible?
questions.a: When its columns are linearly independent (equivalently rows, determinant nonzero).

questions.q: What is the pseudo-inverse of A with independent columns?
questions.a: A† = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T (a left inverse).

questions.q: What is the practical way to solve A x = b?
questions.a: Use a factorization/solver (QR or LU), not by forming A^{-1}.

questions.q: What does A† b give?
questions.a: The least squares solution of A x ≈ b.

modules.exercise: Compare np.linalg.pinv(A) @ b to np.linalg.lstsq(A, b) for a tall A.
modules.recap: Invertible square systems have unique solutions; compute them with factorizations. The pseudo-inverse generalizes the inverse to non-square matrices and solves least squares.

modules.title: ENGR108 L33: VMLS least squares

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 33 - VMLS least squares

read: VMLS 12.1 Least squares problem, 12.2 Solution, 12.3 Solving least squares problems

questions.q: What does least squares minimize?
questions.a: ||A x - b||^2, the sum of squared residuals.

questions.q: What are the normal equations?
questions.a: A^T A x = A^T b.

questions.q: Why is the residual orthogonal to the columns of A at the solution?
questions.a: The gradient of ||Ax-b||^2 vanishes: A^T(Ax-b)=0.

modules.exercise: Fit y = a + b t to 3 points by solving the normal equations by hand.
modules.recap: Least squares finds the x making A x closest to b; the solution satisfies the normal equations and leaves a residual orthogonal to range(A).

modules.title: ENGR108 L34-35: VMLS least squares ex. / VMLS LS data fitting

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 34-VMLS least squares ex.
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 35-VMLS LS data fitting

questions.q: Give an example of least squares for estimation.
questions.a: E.g. estimating a position from many noisy range measurements.

questions.q: What is the model-fitting setup?
questions.a: Choose a model f(x) = sum theta_j f_j(x) and pick theta minimizing sum of squared prediction errors on data.

questions.q: Why does having more measurements than unknowns give least squares?
questions.a: Overdetermined systems have no exact solution, so we minimize the error.

questions.q: What is the RMS error?
questions.a: sqrt(mean of squared residuals).

modules.exercise: Fit a line to 50 noisy points with the formula and np.linalg.lstsq; confirm they agree. (Month 1 practice task.)
modules.recap: Least squares is the workhorse for fitting and estimation from redundant noisy data. Data fitting is linear in the parameters theta; least squares gives the best fit.

modules.title: Practice: Least squares line fit
modules.steps: Install Python with NumPy and Jupyter. Generate 50 noisy points around a line, fit the line using the normal-equations formula by hand, then with np.linalg.lstsq, and check that you get the same answer.

questions.q: What are the normal equations?
questions.a: A^T A x = A^T b.

questions.q: Why is lstsq preferred over inverting A^T A?
questions.a: It's more numerically stable (uses QR/SVD).

questions.q: What does the residual look like when the fit is good?
questions.a: Small and uncorrelated with the columns of A.

modules.exercise: Print both coefficient vectors and assert np.allclose.
modules.recap: Least squares by formula and by library should agree; least squares reappears in sensor calibration.

modules.title: ENGR108 L36: VMLS fit univariate fnc

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 36-VMLS fit univariate fnc

read: VMLS 13.1 Least squares data fitting (univariate functions)

questions.q: How can you fit a nonlinear curve with linear least squares?
questions.a: Use nonlinear basis functions (e.g. polynomial terms); the model is still linear in the coefficients.

questions.q: What goes wrong with very high-degree polynomials?
questions.a: Overfitting: low training error but poor generalization.

questions.q: Reflection: state the main idea of this segment in 2-3 sentences. What would you ask the instructor?
questions.a: Personal check. If you cannot summarise it, rewatch the last 5 minutes of the segment and re-read the textbook section.

modules.exercise: Fit polynomials of degree 1, 3, 9 to noisy sine data and compare residuals.
modules.recap: Choose basis functions; the fitting remains a linear least squares problem.

modules.title: ENGR108 L37: VMLS validation

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 37 - VMLS validation

questions.q: What is the purpose of a validation set?
questions.a: To estimate error on unseen data and detect overfitting.

questions.q: What does it mean if train RMS is small and test RMS is large?
questions.a: The model is overfit and does not generalize.

questions.q: Reflection: state the main idea of this segment in 2-3 sentences. What would you ask the instructor?
questions.a: Personal check. If you cannot summarise it, rewatch the last 5 minutes of the segment and re-read the textbook section.

modules.exercise: Split your noisy dataset 80/20 and plot train vs test error vs polynomial degree.
modules.recap: Always evaluate on held-out data; generalization, not training fit, is what matters.

modules.title: ENGR108 L38-39: VMLS classification / VMLS LS classification

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 38 - VMLS classification
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 39-VMLS LS classification

questions.q: What is a Boolean (two-class) classifier?
questions.a: A function predicting a label +1/-1 from features.

questions.q: How does the least squares classifier work?
questions.a: Fit f(x)=x^T beta + v to +/-1 labels by least squares and predict sign(f(x)).

questions.q: Name the four outcomes in a confusion matrix.
questions.a: True positive, false negative, false positive, true negative.

questions.q: Why is this not the ideal loss for classification?
questions.a: It penalizes confidently correct predictions; logistic or hinge losses fit better, but LS is simple and often works.

modules.exercise: Fit an LS classifier on 2 Gaussian blobs in 2D and plot the boundary.
modules.recap: Classification outputs discrete labels; performance is summarized by the confusion matrix. Regress on +/-1 labels and take the sign: a baseline classifier from least squares.

modules.title: ENGR108 L40-41: VMLS multiclass classif / VMLS multi objective LS

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 40-VMLS multiclass classif
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 41-VMLS multi objective LS

questions.q: How does one-versus-others multiclass work?
questions.a: Train one binary classifier per class and predict the class with the largest score.

questions.q: What does multi-objective LS minimize?
questions.a: A weighted sum J1 + lambda J2 of competing squared objectives.

questions.q: What is the confusion matrix for K classes?
questions.a: A KxK table of predicted versus true counts.

questions.q: What does varying lambda trace out?
questions.a: The trade-off (Pareto) curve between the objectives.

modules.exercise: Minimize ||Ax-b||^2 + lambda ||x||^2 for several lambda and plot both terms.
modules.recap: Multiclass classifiers combine several binary scores via argmax. Weighted sums let you trade off competing goals; the weight lambda sets the balance.

modules.title: ENGR108 L42-43: ctrl via multi obj LS / MLS est & inversion

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 42-ctrl via multi obj LS
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 43-MLS est & inversion

questions.q: How is control posed as multi-objective LS?
questions.a: Minimize tracking error of outputs plus lambda times input energy, with y = A u.

questions.q: What is the inversion/estimation setup?
questions.a: Measurements y = A x + v; estimate x from y despite noise.

questions.q: Why penalize input size?
questions.a: To keep actuator effort small and avoid unrealistically large commands.

questions.q: Why add a regularization term?
questions.a: A prior on x stabilizes the estimate when A is ill-conditioned or noisy.

modules.exercise: Deblur a 1D signal with and without regularization.
modules.recap: Choosing inputs to trade tracking error against effort is the same idea as optimal control costs, previewing LQR. Estimation by regularized least squares balances fitting the data with plausibility of x.

modules.title: ENGR108 L44-45: VMLS reg data fitting / VMLS constrained LS

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 44-VMLS reg data fitting
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 45-VMLS constrained LS

questions.q: How does regularization help data fitting?
questions.a: Penalizing ||theta||^2 shrinks coefficients and reduces overfitting.

questions.q: What is the constrained least squares problem?
questions.a: Minimize ||A x - b||^2 subject to C x = d.

questions.q: How do you choose lambda?
questions.a: By validation: pick the lambda with lowest validation error.

questions.q: Give an example of a natural equality constraint.
questions.a: E.g. forcing a trajectory to pass through a specified final position.

modules.exercise: Fit a line through noisy points that must pass through the origin.
modules.recap: Regularization (ridge) controls model complexity, tuned on a validation set. Constraints enforce hard requirements; least squares then only trades off the remaining error.

modules.title: ENGR108 L46, 48: VMLS solve cstr LS prob / VMLS linear quadrt ctrl

watch.title: Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 46-VMLS solve cstr LS prob
Stanford ENGR108: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra | 2020 | Lecture 48-VMLS linear quadrt ctrl

read: VMLS 16.2 Solution, 16.3 Solving constrained least squares problems

questions.q: What are the optimality (KKT) conditions here?

questions.a: Choose inputs u_t to minimize a quadratic cost on states and inputs subject to linear dynamics x_{t+1}=A x_t + B u_t.

questions.q: How is the problem solved numerically?
questions.a: Solve the KKT system or use QR factorizations.

questions.q: Why is this a constrained least squares problem?

questions.q: How does nonlinear least squares differ from linear?
questions.a: The residual f(x) is nonlinear in x, so there is no closed-form solution.

questions.a: It has the same constrained LS structure, with unknown states instead of inputs.

questions.q: What does Gauss-Newton do at each step?
questions.a: Linearizes f around the current x and solves the resulting linear LS problem.

questions.q: What is nonlinear model fitting?
questions.a: Fitting parameters that enter the model nonlinearly (e.g. exponentials) by minimizing squared residuals.

questions.q: What does Levenberg-Marquardt add?
questions.a: A damping term lambda ||x - x_k||^2 that keeps steps in the trust region where the linearization is valid.

questions.q: Why are initial guesses important?
questions.a: LM only finds local minima.

modules.recap: Repeatedly linearize and solve a least squares problem; LM adds damping for robustness. Numerical IK uses exactly this idea. Nonlinear model fitting = nonlinear LS on parameters, typically solved by LM from a good starting guess.

questions.a: Minimize ||f||^2 + mu ||g||^2 with increasing mu.

questions.q: Why is it harder than the linear case?
questions.a: Both objective and constraint are nonlinear; algorithms are iterative.

questions.q: What advantage does the augmented Lagrangian have?
questions.a: It converges without driving mu to infinity, which avoids ill-conditioning.

It builds directly on Month 2 (CS223A kinematics, Jacobians, force control) and Month 4 (AA203 planning/control); Lecture 18 (behavior cloning) is the idea behind ALOHA, Diffusion Policy and pi0 and pairs with Month 5's CS224R imitation-learning modules. modules.title: Sidebar: the humanoid robotics career map (412 job posts)
modules.steps: From @0x_meden's X Article "I read 412 humanoid robot jobs. Here's the real career map." (Oct 2026; 412 roles at Figure, 1X, Agility, Apptronik, Skild AI and Physical Intelligence). Only 2 of 412 require a PhD; 160 (39%) mention no degree at all. In engineering roles: Python 50%, C++ 32%, PyTorch 11%, ROS 7.5%, MuJoCo/Isaac 7.1%, RL 5.8%, imitation learning 5.8%. Median posted pay for AI/ML roles: $200K–$305.5K. Career ladder: data collection operator (1X, $28–36/hr) → service technician (Figure, $35–65/hr) → Robot Operator II (Agility, $102–133K) → AI researcher (1X, $200–300K) → staff teleop engineer (Agility, $190–296K) → Helix AI engineer (Figure, $200–400K). 12-month plan: months 1–2 Python, Linux, Stanford ENGR108; 3–4 CS223A + MuJoCo; 5–6 C++, AA203 control, then RL; 7–8 SO-101 arm ($122–230) + 50 LeRobot demos + an imitation policy; 9 measure success rate and robustness and write up the failures; 10–12 apply via operator, technician, residency or internship roles. Figures are the author's; check current postings.

questions.a: An SO-101 arm, 50 LeRobot demos, a trained imitation policy, and a write-up of its success rate, robustness and failures.
